To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

• Students’ assertions about a particular conceptual science idea (i.e. their assertions about the concept of buoyancy) are often poorly supported by evidence, and • Students’ assertions that are well supported by evidence are rarely accompanied by rich conceptual talk.

(1) students’ assertions about a particular scientific concept consist primarily of well-supported scientific arguments, but (2) these arguments rarely amount to or conjoined with rich conceptual talk.
(1) students' conceptual talk is not well-supported by argumentation, and (2) students' conceptual arguments are not richly conceptual.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to design and support formative assessment practices that engage students in conceptually rich discussion and that are effective in promoting science learning.
the design and use of discussion-centered formative assessments to support science teaching and learning.
how students learn science concepts through discussion and how discussion supports science teaching.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
discussion is a powerful tool for teaching and learning science and that it is a tool that can be used in many different ways and for many different purposes.

argumentation is a powerful tool in science education, but that its use in classrooms should be guided by an understanding of the different forms it can take, and by a critical analysis of the ways in which its use can support or undermine science learning.
the use of conceptually rich discussion in the classroom has been shown to be an effective method to improve student understanding and achievement of science concepts (Cohen et al., 1999).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the argumentation approach is not a magic bullet for science teaching and learning.

students' reasoning from evidence is not well connected to their conceptual knowledge, and that this lack of connection is a significant challenge for the design of formative assessment in the context of scientific argumentation.
we have developed and tested an approach to teaching science that is effective and efficient, and that can be used to help students develop a deep understanding of science concepts and processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way in which we think about argumentation in science classrooms needs to change.
teachers should use argumentation as a means to an end, not an end in and of itself.

rich, conceptually focused discussion is an essential component of a successful argumentation-based formative assessment process, and that the design of such a process needs to take into consideration the ways in which the argumentation framework and the formative assessment process interact to support student learning.
